## Step 1: Explain the script

```{.r code-line-numbers="false"}
# Map recorded fatal terrorist attacks in London from 2010 to 2018. # <1>
```

1. Start by explaining what the script does. In this case the comment identifies the type of crime, the place and the date range, so that it will be easier to find the script if we want to use it again later. See [Organising code with comments](https://books.lesscrime.info/learncrimemapping/2026/05_your_second_crime_map/index.html#sec-comments).

## Step 2: Load packages

```{.r code-line-numbers="false"}
# Load packages
pacman::p_load(here, httr2, sf, sfhotspot, tidyverse) # <2>
```

2. `pacman::p_load()` loads the packages needed for this analysis, listed in alphabetical order with the tidyverse package last. **[here](https://here.r-lib.org/)** allows us to specify where to find files in the workspace; **[httr2](https://httr2.r-lib.org)** downloads data from the internet; **[sf](https://r-spatial.github.io/sf/)** handles spatial objects; **[sfhotspot](https://pkgs.lesscrime.info/sfhotspot/)** creates crime maps and estimates density; **[tidyverse](https://tidyverse.tidyverse.org)** provides tools for reading, wrangling and plotting data. Loading packages at the start makes it easy to check which tools the script needs. See [Loading packages](https://books.lesscrime.info/learncrimemapping/2026/02_your_first_crime_map/index.html#sec-loading-packages).

## Step 3: Download the original data

```{.r code-line-numbers="false"}
# Download the original data and keep a local copy
request("https://mpjashby.github.io/crimemappingdata/london_attacks.csv") |> # <3>
  req_perform(path = here("data", "raw", "london_attacks.csv")) # <4>
```

3. `request()` specifies the URL of the file to download. The pipe operator (`|>`) passes that request to the next function. This exercise uses one CSV file containing the locations of fatal terrorist attacks in London. See [Downloading and loading data](https://books.lesscrime.info/learncrimemapping/2026/02_your_first_crime_map/index.html#sec-load-data); [Stringing functions together](https://books.lesscrime.info/learncrimemapping/2026/04_transforming_data/index.html#sec-pipe-operator).
4. `req_perform()` performs the download. `here()` specifies where the original file should be saved, relative to the `crime_mapping` workspace. Keeping the original data in `data/raw` means we can return to it if we make a mistake while wrangling the data. See [Keeping your files organised](https://books.lesscrime.info/learncrimemapping/2026/01_getting_started/index.html#sec-create-project).

## Step 4: Read the downloaded data

```{.r code-line-numbers="false"}
# Read data
attacks <- here("data", "raw", "london_attacks.csv") |> # <5>
  read_csv() # <6>
```

5. `here()` specifies the path to the downloaded CSV file within the workspace. The pipe (`|>`) passes this path to `read_csv()`.
6. `read_csv()` from [readr](https://readr.tidyverse.org) reads the local CSV file. `here()` specifies which file to read, while `<-` stores the result as `attacks`. Keeping this step separate from filtering makes it easy to inspect the original data if we need to check it. See [Loading CSV data](https://books.lesscrime.info/learncrimemapping/2026/03_data_wrangling/index.html#sec-data-wrangling-loading-csv-data); [Naming objects](https://books.lesscrime.info/learncrimemapping/2026/03_data_wrangling/index.html#sec-naming-objects).

## Step 5: Select the requested dates

```{.r code-line-numbers="false"}
# Keep only records within the requested date range, including both ends
attacks_filtered <- filter(attacks, date >= "2010-01-01", date <= "2018-12-31") # <7>
```

7. `filter()` from [dplyr](https://dplyr.tidyverse.org) keeps rows from `attacks` that satisfy both conditions. `>=` includes 1 January 2010 and later dates, while `<=` includes 31 December 2018 and earlier dates. The result is stored as `attacks_filtered`. We filter by date because the exercise asks for 2010–2018; we do not need a second filter for fatalities because the supplied file already contains fatal attacks. See [Filtering rows](https://books.lesscrime.info/learncrimemapping/2026/03_data_wrangling/index.html#sec-filter-data).

## Step 6: Describe the original coordinates

```{.r code-line-numbers="false"}
# Convert longitude and latitude to a spatial object
attacks_sf <- st_as_sf( # <8>
  attacks_filtered, # <9>
  coords = c("longitude", "latitude"), # <10>
  crs = "EPSG:4326" # <11>
)
```

8. `st_as_sf()` creates a spatial object and stores it as `attacks_sf`. This tells R that the coordinate columns describe locations on the Earth’s surface. See [Converting data to an SF object](https://books.lesscrime.info/learncrimemapping/2026/05_your_second_crime_map/index.html#sec-your-second-crime-map-converting-our-data-to-an-sf-object).
9. Use the filtered records, rather than the original data, so that only attacks within the requested period are mapped.
10. `coords` names the columns containing the x and y coordinates, in that order. Here the x coordinate is longitude and the y coordinate is latitude.
11. `crs = "EPSG:4326"` specifies how R should interpret the existing longitude and latitude values. It does not transform those coordinates into a different system.

## Step 7: Transform the coordinates

```{.r code-line-numbers="false"}
# Transform to a projected coordinate reference system suitable for London
attacks_sf_trans <- st_transform(attacks_sf, crs = "EPSG:27700") # <12>
```

12. `st_transform()` converts the coordinates in `attacks_sf` to the British National Grid, a projected CRS suitable for London. Unlike the previous step, this changes the coordinates themselves. The result is stored as `attacks_sf_trans`. See [Transforming the coordinate reference system](https://books.lesscrime.info/learncrimemapping/2026/02_your_first_crime_map/index.html#sec-your-first-crime-map-transforming-the-coordinate-reference-system).

## Step 8: Draw the map

```{.r code-line-numbers="false"}
# Display the map
hotspot_map( # <13>
  attacks_sf_trans, # <14>
  basemap_type = "cartolight", # <15>
  colour = "red2", # <16>
  size = 5 # <17>
)
```

13. `hotspot_map()` plots the spatial data over a base map. Leaving the result unassigned means running this final expression displays the map. Different choices of colour and point size could also produce a good answer. See [Drawing the map](https://books.lesscrime.info/learncrimemapping/2026/02_your_first_crime_map/index.html#sec-drawing-first-map).
14. Use the transformed spatial object, which contains only the records selected earlier.
15. A light `cartolight` base map helps readers locate the attacks without distracting from the points. See [Base maps](https://books.lesscrime.info/learncrimemapping/2026/07_map_context/index.html#sec-base-maps).
16. Use red points to give the attacks a strong contrast with the light base map. The points should be more prominent than the streets beneath them. See [Visual hierarchy](https://books.lesscrime.info/learncrimemapping/2026/07_map_context/index.html#sec-visual-hierarchy).
17. Set the point size to 5 so that these relatively few incidents can be seen clearly. A size that works for this map might obscure the pattern in a dataset containing thousands of incidents. See [Controlling aesthetics](https://books.lesscrime.info/learncrimemapping/2026/05_your_second_crime_map/index.html#sec-aesthetics).
